list.listitem: In all patients with a suspected abdominal injury, conduct a primary and secondary survey and a focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST) examination. C
Physical examination is not reliable in patients who are not clinically stable and have abnormal vital signs, examination, or mental status. B

CT is recommended in patients who are hemodynamically stable and have possible abdominal tenderness, a "seatbelt sign," a positive FAST or diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL), or the presence of extraabdominal injuries. B

CT of the abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast is the modality of choice to exclude solid organ and retroperitoneal injury. Although increasingly used for bowel, diaphragm, and pancreas injury, it is not as sensitive in ruling out hollow viscous injuries. B

background.definition: A serious injury or wound inflicted on the abdominal cavity, defined as the region between the diaphragm and inguinal creases vertically and anterior axillary lines laterally. In addition to the anterior trunk, the abdominal cavity can be reached via penetrating injury through the back, buttocks, and flank. Missed or delayed recognition of injuries in abdominal trauma result in significant morbidity and mortality.

list.listitem: The incidence of nonfirearm-related cuts/piercings in adults is 866 per 100,000 compared with 3.3 per 100,000 for firearms, but firearms are associated with fatality 6 times more than stab wounds.
Children between the ages of 0 and 14 years have a much lower incidence of penetrating injuries compared with adults.
Stab wounds more commonly occur in the upper abdominal quadrants and on the left more than the right.
Blunt abdominal trauma is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in adults and children. It results in greater mortality than penetrating trauma in adults.
Blunt abdominal trauma is often difficult to diagnose clinically and is associated with multiple injuries to other body parts, which can further complicate management.
Motor vehicle accidents (MVA) and auto versus pedestrian accidents are the major cause of blunt abdominal trauma, especially in unrestrained individuals.

The 3-point shoulder-lap belt is most protective for sustaining abdominal injuries. The use of shoulder belts alone has the same mortality as using no seatbelt, and although effective in reducing mortality, the use of a solitary lap belt can result in significant intraabdominal injury.
Children are at greater risk of sustaining intraabdominal injury in blunt abdominal trauma because of their smaller body habitus, weaker musculature, and greater proportional organ size.
In both children and adults with blunt abdominal trauma, the liver, spleen, and kidneys are the most commonly affected organs.

Blunt abdominal trauma causes an abrupt rise in intraabdominal pressure, which in turn may cause rupture of hollow organs. Compression of viscera between anterior force and posterior vertebral column and thoracic cage may also cause crush injury to solid organs such as liver and spleen. Rapid acceleration/deceleration forces can tear fixed vascular structures such as pedicles and the aorta.

Blunt abdominal trauma can result in significant volume loss that can result in hypotension and altered mentation. Enteric contamination may result from leakage of acidic, enzymatic, and hematic contents, producing peritonitis and abdominal tenderness and rigidity.
An abdominal bruise, the "seatbelt sign," or the presence of extraabdominal injuries suggests intraabdominal injury. B

The focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST) examination or diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) can be used as an initial diagnostic tool. DPL is more time and labor intensive and has a greater complication rate, whereas the FAST examination may be less sensitive depending on the user. B
Clinically unstable patients and those with an abnormal mentation have an unreliable abdominal examination. Clinically stable patients with abdominal tenderness should be further evaluated with CT. B

Abdominal CT with IV contrast accurately identifies hemoperitoneum among patients with blunt abdominal trauma; oral contrast is no longer recommended. Although sensitive, CT alone cannot exclude bowel, diaphragm, or pancreas injury. B

If a patient has normal vital signs, has normal mental status, and appears stable, then obtain a brief history about the event. Elicit age, medical history, and information about the incident. If a fall from a height, the approximate length and landing platform; if MVA, then the type of collision, vehicle type, speed, use of seatbelt, deployment of airbag, presence of fatalities at the scene, presence of passenger space intrusion, and use of extrication by rescue personnel.

Patients at greater risk for having severe abdominal injury are the very old and very young, with smaller body habitus, lacking appropriate seatbelt use, and with presentation of other bodily injuries. For motor vehicle collisions, lacking appropriate seatbelt use, being involved in a rollover collision, being ejected from the vehicle, or having a death at the scene is highly associated with significant abdominal injury.
Ask patients about anticoagulation and consider reversal if appropriate.
The most common affected organ of bicycle handlebar injuries is the liver. It is associated with abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, and an imprint on the abdomen.

Vitals: Hypotension most likely is due to volume loss caused by hemorrhaging from a solid organ or vascular source. Tachycardia can be an early indicator of hemorrhaging or may be attributable to pain and emotional shock.

Examination: A complete primary and secondary assessment must be conducted on all patients along with a bedside hemoglobin and blood glucose level. In a patient who has altered mental status, physical examination is inaccurate in evaluating blunt abdominal trauma. In a patient who is awake and alert, a thorough abdominal examination involves auscultation and visual examination for distention, discoloration of the skin, obvious wounds, and bruising followed by palpation of the anterior abdominal wall from the costal margins to the inguinal ligaments, palpation of bilateral flanks from costal margins to the iliac wings, and palpation of the back from the costal margins to the iliac wings. Palpation should elicit tenderness, guarding, or rebound. The examination should also include assessment of the anterior, lateral, posterior ribs, and pelvis for fracture.

The clinical assessment is specific but not very sensitive for intraabdominal injury. Distention, guarding, and the "seatbelt sign" (visible bruising on the abdominal wall) are useful for ruling in intraabdominal injury, but absence of these or other symptoms does not rule it out. A positive seatbelt sign was associated with a higher likelihood of intraabdominal injury (OR 3.6) and increased need for surgical intervention (OR 7.3).
Persistent pain for 2 or more hours is an independent predictor of intraabdominal injury in children.

Presence of GCS <14, guarding, or tenderness is more sensitive (68%) but less specific. A complaint of abdominal pain or findings of abdominal tenderness is even more sensitive (82%) but even less specific.

The presence of extraabdominal injury can be highly correlated with concerning intraabdominal injury. Especially in patients who may not complain of abdominal pain or have abdominal tenderness on examination, the presence of a "distracting injury," such as a long-bone fracture or chest contusion, can be an important indicator for the presence of intraabdominal injury. In a study evaluating patients without complaints of abdominal pain or intraabdominal injury, all the patients who were found to have intraabdominal injuries (10/142) were found to have distracting injuries.
Mesenteric avulsion is rare but has a 15% mortality. Patients typically have diffuse abdominal tenderness followed by bruising.
Once a part of routine trauma evaluation, the digital rectal exam has very low sensitivity for intraabdominal injuries and is not recommended as a screening tool.

For blunt trauma, diagnosis is aimed at detecting hemoperitoneum and source of hemorrhage, as well as identifying any hollow or solid organ that would require operative intervention. Evaluation and diagnosis of a patient with suspected abdominal trauma with intraperitoneal injury should include a history and physical, FAST exam, or diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) and CT, and possibly exploratory laparotomy, operative repair of an organ, or angiography for the arterial embolization of bleeding vessels.

As part of the initial assessment, a FAST exam, if readily feasible and quickly accessible, should be conducted by an experienced user on all patients who are at risk for abdominal injury as part of the initial assessment. The FAST exam is preferred over DPL in evaluating for hemoperitoneum because it is noninvasive and is more time efficient. A FAST exam is highly accurate for predicting intraabdominal injury based on a study with 245 trauma patients (LR+ 90, LR- 0.1).

If a patient is hemodynamically stable, has a normal mental status and examination, and has a negative FAST examination, but complains of abdominal pain or has tenderness on examination, the patient should receive a CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast. CT of abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast no longer requires PO contrast to assess bowel or mesenteric injuries. If the patient has no complaints of pain, is not tender on examination, does not have a distracting injury, and has an otherwise normal examination, then the patient can be observed for 4 hours and reexamined prior to being sent home. Previous studies have found that addition of CXR and 3 laboratory parameters (WBC count, hematocrit, and aspartate aminotransferase) could improve the ability to exclude intraabdominal injury.

A study of 754 patients with abdominal seatbelt sign found hollow viscus injury (HVI) in 9.2% (n=69). Only 1 did not have one of the following 8 CT findings: abdominal wall soft tissue contusion, free fluid, bowel wall thickening, mesenteric stranding, mesenteric hematoma, bowel dilation, pneumatosis, or pneumoperitoneum. The finding most strongly associated with HVI was the presence of free fluid (OR 43).

If all other sources of instability have been addressed and a patient is not hemodynamically stable or has altered mental status after sustaining a blunt abdominal injury, then the patient must be taken immediately to the operating room with surgical consult.

Laboratory tests: A low hematocrit confirms the presence of hemorrhage, and a low glucose may explain the altered level of consciousness. Additional helpful studies that are not considered part of a trauma evaluation have included blood gas analysis and lactate. Depending on the presentation of the patient, a urine toxicology screen can be obtained.
A study identified SGOT >34 IU/L as an independent predictor of intraabdominal injury in children with blunt abdominal trauma.

However, a study of 323 patients with blunt abdominal trauma of whom 18 had solid organ injury concluded that individual tests were of limited value. There was a significant association between ALT, AST, amylase and lipase and solid organ injury, but the sensitivity and specificity were modest.
Urinalysis: a negative urinalysis is associated with a low risk of intraabdominal or genitourinary injury.

The FAST bedside ultrasound examination is now part of routine diagnostic care for blunt abdominal trauma patients and is preferred over DPL in detecting hemoperitoneum in these patients. By evaluating the 4 windows (hepatorenal, splenorenal, suprapubic, and subxiphoid views), the FAST examination can provide quick, accurate information about the presence of intraperitoneal fluid, aiding in the management decision. The FAST examination is not helpful in evaluating bowel, diaphragmatic, or mesentery injuries, along with retroperitoneal bleeding. The accuracy of the FAST examination does rely on the expertise of the user, and evidence of mortality benefit is lacking.

A systematic review found 4 high quality studies with 4263 patients that evaluated the accuracy of POCUS FAST for detection of intraabdominal injury in a disaster or mass casualty setting. Overall it was 92% sensitive and 98.7% specific (LR+ 70, LR- 0.08). A Cochrane review found POCUS to be helpful in treament decisions when positive for patients with blunt thoracoabdominal trauma. However, a negative POCUS in patients with abdominal trauma does not accurately exclude injuries, hence a CT may still be warranted especially in pediatric trauma where the sensitivity of POCUS is low. POCUS may be more accurate for thoracic trauma but this needs verification in larger studies.

Contrast-enhanced ultrasound has similar accuracy. A systematic review identified 9 studies with sample sizes from 22 to 392 patients and a sensitivity of 92% and specificity of 98% (LR+ 35, LR- 0.08).

Plain films: The presence of a pelvic fracture or disruption in the pelvic ring suggests the presence of visceral organ damage and potential retroperitoneal bleeding. The CXR can be useful in the assessment of abdominal trauma, as it can identify additional trauma, such as fractured ribs or pneumothoraces, which could suggest more sever injury.

Computed tomography: The CT examination is routinely used to assess for injury in the intraperitoneum, retroperitoneum, and spine in a clinically stable patient. The use of oral contrast is no longer recommended because it delays the completion of the study, does not increase accuracy, and has potential complications such as aspiration. The use of IV contrast enhances the ability of the CT to detect solid organ damage, along with the source of intraperitoneal bleeding. It is also reasonably sensitive in evaluating bowel and mesentary injuries.If a patient remains stable and does not have any other concerning injuries or complaints, a negative CT scan can suggest that the patient can be discharged home. A Cochrane review did not find RCTs evaluating the difference between routine versus selective thoracoabdominal CT in evaluating patients with blunt high-energy trauma.

Angiography: Angiography embolization is an alternative to surgery for diagnosis and management of pelvic and peritoneal bleeding. Patients with pelvic trauma require angiography to occlude bleeding pelvic vessels. Recently, the use of angiography is also extending to the abdomen. The procedure does require a team of specialists and on-call angiography personnel, who are often not available in hospitals. When used, angiography is 96% to 100% successful in diagnosing and achieving vessel occlusion.

Introduced in 1964, this open or closed diagnostic procedure involving the aspiration of peritoneal fluid or washing of the peritoneal cavity with saline is being replaced increasingly with the FAST examination. Clinical decisions with DPL must be based on the aspiration of gross blood or the microscopic evaluation of the lavage fluid.

Although very sensitive, DPL is labor and time intensive along with having potential complications (1%-2%) and thus is no longer recommended. Notably, when used in conjunction with CT, DPL has been found to have a much lower exploratory laparotomy rate.

The PECARN 5 variable clinical prediction rule can rule out serious injury in children following blunt abdominal trauma; it uses the history and physical, lab tests, and chest x-ray and has been prospectively validated.

A second PECARN risk score does not require laboratory or imaging and has been prospectively validated in children with blunt abdominal injury with negative predictive value of 99.9% for ruling out need for acute intervention.

Children with none of the following criteria are at very low risk (0.6%) for intraabdominal injury, of whom 0/743 required intervention. The criteria are: AST >200 U/L Abdominal wall trauma, tenderness, or distension Abnormal chest radiograph Complaint of abdominal pain Abnormal pancreatic enzymes (lipase or amylase)
See for a suggested approach to management of blunt abdominal trauma.

Patients who are hemodynamically unstable require 2 large-bore IVs and continuous but not overly aggressive fluid resuscitation. Consider blood products if the patient is severely hypotensive in a 1:1 ratio with fresh frozen plasma. C
Patients with possible pelvic trauma and hemodynamic instability should have angiographic embolization. B

Patients who are hemodynamically unstable with a positive FAST or diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) should have an exploratory laparotomy. Depending on the type of intraabdominal injury, patients may obtain nonoperative management for certain types of splenic and liver injuries. Hollow viscus injuries (HVIs) require operative repair. B
A study of 9265 children with acute intraabdominal injury found that only 16% were managed operatively. The most commonly injured organs were liver (39%) and spleen (32%).
A clinically unstable patient with a positive FAST ultrasound or DPL examination for intraperitoneal blood must immediately have an exploratory laparotomy.
Consider retroperitoneal hemorrhage and pelvic angiography in a clinically unstable patient with radiographic signs of pelvic trauma and no signs of intraperitoneal bleeding.

A clinically stable patient with a positive FAST or DPL can be sent to CT, and the decision for laparotomy or angiography can be made after more is known about the injury. If the CT reveals splenic or liver injury, nonoperative management may be appropriate, depending on the injury. Hollow visceral injury, such as of bowel or diaphragm, requires immediate surgical repair.

A systematic review comparing early versus delayed intervention for patients with hollow viscus injury following blunt abdominal trauma found no difference in mortality (17% in both groups) but higher morbidity with delayed surgery.

In hemodynamically unstable patients, fluid resuscitation should be initiated. There is controversy about whether the resuscitation should be aggressive, continuous, or delayed, and whether the fluid should be hypertonic or normal saline. Given the lack of convincingly supportive literature for delayed treatment and the presence of some literature questioning aggressive treatment and supporting continuous treatment, continuous IVF administration with normal saline to maintain a blood pressure above 50 mm Hg systolic is recommended.
Ask patients about anticoagulation and consider reversal if appropriate.

If pressure is at or below 50 mm Hg systolic, patient has altered sensorium, or any concern for bleeding, aggressive fluid resuscitation along with a 1:1 ratio of blood products and fresh frozen plasma should be initiated.
If a patient is hypoglycemic, start IV dextrose.
If a patient has sustained a wound or abrasion on the abdomen or any other part of the body, consider updating tetanus immunization.
There have been no randomized studies of the effectiveness of administering prophylactic antibiotics for penetrating abdominal trauma.
For patients with hepatic trauma, angioembolization was effective (93%) but had major complications for some patients including hepatic necrosis (15%), abscess (7%) and bile leaks.
A systematic review found 8 studies with 210 patients who were managed non-operatively. The success rate was 92.4% with 4.6% mortality and a 9.7% complication rate.

A systematic review of case reports identified 51 reports of 66 patients who sustained an extrahepatic bile duct injury following blunt trauma, most commonly suprapancreatic common bile duct (CBD) in 29%, complete transection of the intrapancreatic CBD in 23%, and partial laceration of the left hepatic duct in 20%. Late diagnosis (mean 11 days) was common in hemodynamically stable patients managed non-operatively.
A Cochrane review found no RCTs evaluating nonoperative versus operative management of high-grade blunt liver injury.

A systematic review of 8 studies with 2135 children being evaluated following blunt abdominal trauma found that a POCUS FAST examination had high specificity but low sensitivity (LR+ 10.8, LR- 0.6) for detection of intra-abdominal injury. Thus, a positive exam means intra-abdominal injury is likely, while a negative exam requires further diagnostic evaluation and imaging.

Implementation of an evidence-based guideline to reduce CT use in children 0 to 15 years with blunt abdominal trauma successfully reduced the rate from 48.3% before implementation to 36.7% after, with no adverse effect on outcomes.

A systematic review identified 42 observational studies with 1754 children who had experienced blunt pancreatic trauma. Most were initially managed non-operatively and had the same mortality as those managed operatively. Selection of appropriate patients is of course important. The only difference was a higher incidence of pseudocysts in those managed non-operatively.

Traumatic abdominal wall hernia in children is most commonly caused by bicycle handlebars, although non-bicycle injuries were more likely to have intraabdominal injuries (61% vs 33%). Most patients were managed using laprascopic surgery.

cell.label: Extensive car damage, passenger space intruded by vehicle, or air bag deployment?
Alert and oriented, normal vital signs, negative FAST, and normal AP pelvis (if ordered)?
Conduct more thorough exam; abdominal tenderness or pain, "seatbelt sign" (bruise on the abdomen), or history of coagulopathy?
CT abdomen pelvis with IV contrast and consider surgery consult.
Consider observing patient for 4 to 6 hours if there are concerning mechanisms; if patient remains stable, then discharge home.
Intubate and ventilate; IV fluids (adult at least 1-2 L NS bolus, pediatric NS bolus at 40 cc/kg; type and cross O-negative blood blood).
Call surgery to prepare the operating room; if patient is unstable, must go immediately to the OR.
Obtain CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast and obtain surgery consult immediately.
Obtain CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast and inform interventional radiology to prepare for angiography.
Patient with suspected blunt abdominal trauma: secure airway, breathing, circulation; IV access and fluid resuscitation; examine for other important injuries.
